title: Axial gravitational perturbations and echo-like signals of a hairy black hole from gravitational decoupling
summary: We study axial gravitational perturbations of a hairy black hole constructed in the framework of gravitational decoupling and investigate the geometric origin of echo-like late-time signals in this spacetime. We derive the odd-parity master equation and the corresponding effective potential, and we compute the quasinormal-mode spectrum by using frequency-domain and time-domain methods. We show that, in a suitable region of parameter space, the axial potential develops a double-peak structure that supports a trapping cavity and gives rise to echo-like late-time waveforms. Rather than imposing near-horizon reflectivity by hand, the delayed pulses therefore arise dynamically from the geometry of the effective potential. We also clarify that the parameter region exhibiting echoes need not coincide with the region in which the weak energy condition is satisfied everywhere outside the event horizon, and this distinction must be taken into account when interpreting the physical status of the solution. Our results provide a useful framework for probing black-hole hair through gravitational-wave ringdown and for exploring possible observational departures from the standard no-hair paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates axial gravitational perturbations of a hairy black hole obtained via gravitational decoupling, showing that echo-like late-time signals emerge dynamically from a double-peaked effective potential—without ad hoc near-horizon reflectivity—and clarifies that echo-supporting parameter regions need not satisfy the weak energy condition globally.
AI.motivation: To understand the geometric origin of echo-like late-time signals in hairy black hole spacetimes and assess their viability as observational probes of black hole hair beyond the no-hair theorem.
AI.method: Derivation of the odd-parity master equation and effective potential for axial perturbations; computation of quasinormal modes using both frequency-domain (e.g., continued fraction) and time-domain (e.g., evolution of wave packets) methods; analysis of potential morphology, trapping cavity formation, and energy condition compliance.
AI.result: A double-peaked structure in the axial effective potential arises in a specific parameter regime, enabling quasi-bound states and producing echo-like late-time waveforms; echoes emerge dynamically from geometry—not imposed boundary conditions; echo-supporting parameters do not necessarily satisfy the weak energy condition everywhere outside the horizon.
AI.conclusion: Echoes in this hairy black hole model are geometrically intrinsic and provide a physically motivated, testable signature of black hole hair; the results establish a framework for using ringdown observations to constrain deviations from general relativity and the no-hair paradigm.

title: Quadratic gravity corrections to scalar QNMs of rapidly rotating black holes
summary: In an effective-field-theory framework for gravity, black-hole quasinormal mode spectra acquire corrections in quadratic-curvature, scalar-tensor extensions of general relativity. Previous calculations of such corrections were limited to moderate spins, since the corresponding background solutions relied on expansions in the spin parameter. Using recently constructed numerical black-hole solutions valid for large spin, we compute the leading-order deviations from general relativity in the scalar quasinormal mode spectrum of rotating black holes in scalar Gauss-Bonnet and dynamical Chern-Simons gravity. We solve the resulting perturbation equations with pseudo-spectral collocation methods, allowing us to determine the quasinormal-mode corrections for dimensionless spins up to $a/M=0.99$, with accuracy better than $\lesssim 10^{-3}$ for the $l=m=0$ mode and $\lesssim 10^{-6}$ for higher multipoles. For spins $a/M>0.9$, the corrections to certain modes can increase by orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: This paper computes leading-order deviations in scalar quasinormal mode spectra of rapidly rotating black holes in quadratic-curvature, scalar-tensor gravity theories (scalar Gauss-Bonnet and dynamical Chern-Simons), using numerical black-hole backgrounds valid up to spin a/M = 0.99 and pseudo-spectral methods—achieving high accuracy and revealing orders-of-magnitude growth in corrections for spins > 0.9.
AI.motivation: Previous calculations of quasinormal mode corrections in quadratic-curvature, scalar-tensor gravity were limited to moderate black-hole spins due to reliance on spin expansions; this work aims to extend the analysis to near-extremal spins using fully nonlinear numerical solutions.
AI.method: Uses recently constructed numerical rotating black-hole solutions in scalar Gauss-Bonnet and dynamical Chern-Simons gravity (valid for large spin), solves linear scalar perturbation equations with pseudo-spectral collocation methods, and computes complex quasinormal mode frequencies for multipoles including l=m=0 and higher.
AI.result: Obtains quasinormal-mode corrections with accuracy ≲10⁻³ (l=m=0) and ≲10⁻⁶ (higher multipoles) up to a/M = 0.99; finds that for a/M > 0.9, corrections to certain modes grow by orders of magnitude compared to lower-spin regimes.
AI.conclusion: Quasinormal mode spectroscopy in near-extremal black holes offers significantly enhanced sensitivity to quadratic-curvature, scalar-tensor modifications of general relativity—enabling stronger constraints from gravitational-wave observations.

title: Fluid perturbations from expanding bubbles in first-order phase transitions
summary: We study the power spectrum of the velocity field induced during a first-order phase transition occurring in the radiation-dominated era. We focus on the phase of bubble expansion, assuming that it ends with the onset of the sound-wave regime. The main result we present is a refined template for the velocity spectrum at the beginning of the sound-wave phase, which can be used for studying the resulting anisotropic stresses and gravitational wave production. In particular, we find that the breaks in the velocity spectrum are not associated to the bubble size and the sound shell thickness, as previously proposed, but to the position of the discontinuities. This distinction is particularly relevant for supersonic deflagrations, as it implies that the intermediate slope is more pronounced and the two breaks are more separated when the wall velocity approaches the Chapman-Jouget speed, instead of the sound speed. We also show that the asymptotic branches of the velocity power spectrum are determined by the integral over the single-bubble profiles at large scales, and by the discontinuities of the velocity profiles at small scales. Furthermore, we study the dependence of the two breaks and the intermediate slope on the distribution function of the times of bubble nucleation (exponential and simultaneous). All the results presented in this work have been included in the public Python package CosmoGW.

AI.tldr: This paper refines the velocity power spectrum template for first-order phase transitions in the radiation-dominated era, identifying discontinuity positions—not bubble size or sound shell thickness—as the origin of spectral breaks; it clarifies scale-dependent asymptotics, analyzes wall-velocity and nucleation-time distribution dependencies, and implements results in the public CosmoGW package.
AI.motivation: To improve gravitational wave predictions from cosmological first-order phase transitions by accurately modeling the velocity field power spectrum at the onset of the sound-wave regime, addressing shortcomings in prior templates that misattributed spectral breaks to bubble size and sound shell thickness.
AI.method: Analytical and semi-analytical modeling of the velocity field during bubble expansion, including single-bubble profile integration, discontinuity analysis, and parametric study of wall velocity (especially near Chapman-Jouget speed) and nucleation-time distributions (exponential vs. simultaneous); implementation and validation via the CosmoGW Python package.
AI.result: Spectral breaks originate from velocity profile discontinuities—not bubble radius or sound shell width—leading to enhanced intermediate slope and wider break separation for supersonic deflagrations approaching the Chapman-Jouget speed; large-scale asymptotics arise from integrated single-bubble profiles, small-scale asymptotics from discontinuities; nucleation-time distribution significantly affects break locations and intermediate slope.
AI.conclusion: The refined velocity spectrum template improves accuracy of anisotropic stress and gravitational wave calculations, especially for non-detonative transitions; the discontinuity-based interpretation resolves inconsistencies in prior models and enables robust, physically grounded GW forecasts for future detectors.
